Email the PSAC: gpsac@muni.org, or call the GVSA office at 907-343-8374.

Q: What is the Girdwood Public Safety Advisory Committee?
The Girdwood Public Safety Advisory Committee (PSAC) is a subcommittee of the Girdwood Board of
Supervisors (GBOS). The PSAC was formed in 2016, with the initial purpose of helping to find "right-sized"
policing for our community after the Alaska State Troopers left their Girdwood post. The PSAC's ongoing
purpose is to serve as a conduit between the community and law enforcement. The committee consists of four
volunteer members. PSAC meets with the Girdwood Fire Department, Whittier Police, and Service Area
Manager to discuss safety-related issues impacting our community.

Q: When are the Girdwood Public Safety Advisory Committee Meetings?
A: PSAC meets every other month. The next meeting is scheduled for August 11 at 7PM.

PSAC meetings are publicly noticed online: www.muni.org/gpsac and are physically posted at the Girdwood
Post Office, Gerrish Branch Library, and Girdwood Community Room bulletin boards. Public can contact
PSAC members directly via email links from the webpage, email the PSAC: gpsac@muni.org, or call the
GVSA office at 907-343-8374.

Q: Why does the Whittier Police Department provide police service to Girdwood?
A: Girdwood has partnered with the Whittier Police Department since 2016. Prior to 2016, Girdwood was
policed by the Alaska State Troopers (AST). AST service to Girdwood discontinued due to state budget
limitations. Girdwood residents voted to partner with the Whittier Police Department, and this partnership
continues today.

Q: What geographic area does the Whittier Police Department cover?
A: The Whittier Police Department is responsible for policing the City of Whittier and has a contract with the
Municipality of Anchorage to provide police services within the Girdwood Valley Service Area. According to
Alaska Statute (AS.35.225) all sworn officers are duty-bound to respond to traffic violations committed in their
presence, regardless of location. WPD provides agency assistance to other law enforcement entities upon
request.

Whittier Police Service Information

Q: How do I call for police service?
A: Call 911 for emergencies. Your call is then forwarded to Whittier Police Dispatch if you’re calling from the
Girdwood Valley Service Area or to Anchorage Police Department Dispatch if you are on the Seward Highway
or up Crow Creek Road.
The non-emergency number is 907-783-3223.

Q: Is there a Whittier Police Substation in Girdwood?
A: Yes. The Whittier Police have an office across from Chair 5. The entrance is around the back of the building.
The office is staffed by appointment only. Call 907-783-3223 to make an appointment.

Q: Can Whittier Police write parking and speeding tickets?
A: Yes. Funds generated from parking and speeding tickets goes into the State of Alaska General Fund.

Q: How do Whittier Police know where my house is?
A: Having a clearly marked street address is important for fire, ambulance, and police response. Whittier Police
have been provided Girdwood Maps and Mapbooks from the Municipality of Anchorage (MOA).

Q: Where do arrested individuals go?
A: All arrested individuals will be transported to Anchorage for processing by the Alaska Court System.

Q: How do I get a copy of my police report or file a police report?
A: Complete a request for records at: www.whittieralaska.gov. WPD has an office in the building across from
Chair 5. The entrance is around the back. Call 907-783-3223 to make an appointment.

Q: How do I file a restraining order?
A: Contact Whittier Police Department at 907-783-3223 and they will assist you with the court process.

Q: I need a background check and fingerprints for work, where should I go?
A: You can obtain a background check from the Alaska State Trooper Office in Anchorage on Tudor Road.
There are various private fingerprinting businesses in Anchorage.

To: Girdwood Bear Aware (GBA)

From: Wind River Bear Institute (WRBI)

Proposal Summary: Bear Safety Education Programming for Girdwood in 2027

Wind River Bear Institute proposes two educational programs in partnership with GBA to
strengthen community understanding of bear behavior, improve public safety, and reduce human-
bear conflict in Girdwood for the summer of 2027. These programs were designed to provide
practical skills and memorable educational experiences for both children and adults living and
recreating in bear country, and to build on the work that WRBI, GBA, and Alaska Department of
Fish & Game have collaborated on over the past 6 years.

Program 1: Inert Bear Spray Training with Robotic Bear Platform

Hands-on inert bear spray training using our remote-controlled, bear-on-wheels training platform,
designed to simulate approaching bear encounters in a safe and controlled setting.

Participants practice:
    •   Proper storage, carry, and deployment of bear spray
    •  Drawing and aiming under realistic conditions
    •  Understanding optimal uses of bear spray and limitations
    •   Interpreting common bear behaviors and correct human response

Many people carry bear spray but have never practiced using it. This program converts equipment
into practiced skill and increases participant confidence and preparedness in bear country.

Audience: Adults, recreationists, hunters, and youth
Session Length: 90 minutes
Participants: 30+ participants
Market Value: $2,000.00


                                       1

Program 2: “Think Like a Bear!” – Interactive Bear Safety Demonstration for Kids & Adults

WRBI performs our interactive “Think Like a Bear!” skit for children and adults. The skit uses a
costumed “bear” character together with two of our friendly & engaging Wildlife K-9 teaching
assistants to demonstrate:

    •  How bears learn behaviors through food rewards
    •  How people unintentionally teach bears conflict behaviors
    •   Practical ways to secure attractants around homes and camps
    •  Common bear behaviors and what to do during encounters
    •   Respectful coexistence with wildlife

The skit uses familiar concepts like dog training and food rewards to help kids and adults
understand how human actions influence bear behavior in fun, entertaining, and memorable ways.

Audience: school and preschool aged children & adults
Session Length: 45 minutes
Participants: 50+ participants
Market Value: $1,000.00

Anticipated Outcomes
These programs are intended to:
    •   Increase community confidence and preparedness in bear country
    •  Improve understanding of bear behavior
    •  Reduce human behaviors that lead to conflict with bears
    •  Encourage stewardship and coexistence practices
    •  Support GBA efforts to reduce human-bear conflicts within the community

WRBI appreciates the opportunity and looks forward to continuing its collaborative work with
GBA to help build a safer and more bear-aware community.

Wind River Bear Institute Overview and Background

The Wind River Bear Institute (WRBI) was founded in 1996 by bear biologist, Carrie L. Hunt, to
provide innovative, non-lethal solutions to human-wildlife conflict problems. After testing and
developing the product now known as “bear spray” (perhaps the greatest contribution to the world
of non-lethal bear deterrence of our time), Hunt began experimenting with other aversive
conditioning tools, including the first use of rubber bullets on grizzly bears and on-site “hard”
release technique to teach wild bears to avoid human-occupied space; allowing these animals to
remain on the landscape without having to be relocated or destroyed. This pursuit also led her to
the Karelian Bear Dog (KBD) for preventing and responding to human-wildlife conflicts with a
focus on grizzly bears.

The KBD is a hardy hunting dog from Finland that is renowned for their ability to pursue and bay
large game safely and effectively. Traditional knowledge of the breed indicates that select KBDs
from good hunting lines are fearless even in the pursuit of grizzly bear. Hunt recognized the utility
of KBD for wildlife management and began breeding, testing, selecting, placing, and handling
KBDs under the working title “Wildlife K-9” (WK9).

Taking on the role of conservationist, the highly adaptable WK9 has proven to be a perfect partner
for wildlife managers and as “Wildlife Ambassadors” – bridging the gap between people and
wildlife during education & outreach events. Hunt developed the concept of Bear Shepherding©:
teaching people how to prevent negative encounters with bears while simultaneously using
principles of operant conditioning to teach wild bears behaviorally based life lessons that create
boundary awareness and avoidance of human-occupied space.

Over the past 30+ years of working with Federal, State, and Provincial agencies, as well as private
landowners and industry throughout western North America and Japan, WRBI’s Bear Shepherding
methods and protocols have resulted in hundreds of actions on bears annually by WRBI and our
WK9 Handlers with no resulting injuries to bears, WK9s, or humans.


Our Mission: Advance the use of wildlife K-9 dogs to reduce human-wildlife conflict, improve
public safety, promote wildlife conservation, conduct research, and provide bear safety training
and education to make the world safer for wildlife and people.

Who We Are: Wildlife Biologist, Human-Bear Conflict Specialist – Wildlife K-9 Trainers &
Handlers providing innovative solutions to human-wildlife conflict problems.

Wildlife K-9s: Karelian Bear Dogs (or similar dog) bred, evaluated, selected, trained & handled
by Wildlife Professionals for human-wildlife conflict management and public education.



                                       3

Our Services:


     -  Bear Protection Service:
      Biologist/WK9 Teams patrolling for bears and pushing them away from human-use
        areas, tracking bear activity, managing attractants, providing bear safety education,
       consulting, personnel training, on-site assistance & response.


     -  Bear Management Consulting:
      Bear Hazard Assessments, Human-Bear Conflict Reduction Programs, Bear Management
       Plans.


     -   Personnel Training:
      Bear safety training, safe & effective use of bear deterrents, hazing & aversive
       conditioning techniques, WK9 Training & Handling, Bear Spray Training.


     -  Bear Den Detection:
      Biologist/WK9 Teams paired with FLIR-equipped unmanned aircraft systems to find
       bear dens for research & avoidance (Pedersen et al. 2019).


     -  Dog Training:
       Evaluations, basic to advanced Partnership Training, WK9 Training & Handler
        Certification.


     -  KBD Puppies:
      #1 source of bear working KBDs in North America & Japan! All our puppies are tested,
       evaluated & placed for working aptitude & personality match with owners.


     -  Bear Safety Education & Outreach:
       Friendly & engaging WK9 “Wildlife Ambassadors” bridge the gap between people and
        wildlife, teaching people how to make the world safer for bears & humans!

From:                 Christina Cope Hendrickson
To:                Girdwood Public Safety Advisory Committee
Cc:                     Fisher, Michael R.; Kelley, Kyle T.
Subject:           Fwd: PSAC meeting August 11
Date:              Wednesday, August 5, 2026 2:37:24 PM
Attachments:       image.png

[EXTERNAL EMAIL]

Neighbors,

For the upcoming meeting, I wanted to provide the following public comments:

First, thank you for the focus on the speed limit and use of J Brakes by construction companies
visiting the Girdwood Valley and traveling on Alyeska Highway. Please let me know if you
require any additional citizen engagement on this matter.

Second, I wanted to summarize my Forest Fair observations of Safeway's refrigerator unit that
was parked perpendicular to Hightower Road.

On Friday, 3 July, I contacted the Whittier Police Department.  I witnessed multiple pedestrian
and vehicle interactions along Hightower Road as a result of Safeway's refrigerated truck.  It
was parked perpendicular to Hightower and blocked the sideway and partway into Hightower
Road.

On 3 July, Safeway staff sporadically unloaded items until 10 AM and then closed up the
truck; it remained until Wednesday, 8 July.

Within the municipality, obstructing a collector road requires a permit. Hightower Road is a
collector road. When prompted, Safeway staff conveyed they had no permit because they
would be actively unloading all weekend.  I read up on municipal code, and that's not a true
statement. There was no traffic plan, no cones, no notification, nothing to abate the impact.

In addition to the safety hazard:
1. The truck's refrigeration unit is above the permitted decibels across from a residential
building.
2. The truck blocked multiple businesses' storefronts from potential foot traffic.

On 7 July, I followed up with Whittier Police. They conveyed that an Officer stopped by and
took the active loading comment at face value.  I am disappointed at the lack of code
awareness that gave the office standing to remove/abate the hazard.

From 2025, I recall Safeway's need to have a refrigerated truck last year due to the broken
freezers; that is not the impetus this year. Safeway has another loading dock capability over
by its trash cans.. During Forest Fair, other vendors set up in this space. Safeway should use it
for its intended purpose.

Thanks to Kyle K's prompting, I filed an ANCWorks 240145, which was assigned to Michael
Fisher, copied above for awareness.

Requested Action: that this item be noted for PSAC's 2027 Forest Fair Plan and work with

MOA to permit Safeway to use the loading dock facing Girdwood Place and not Hightower
Road. This aerial view shows more capacity and clearance to permit that action in that
specific space.

GPSAC,

I hope you enjoyed a lovely Forest Fair weekend. On Friday, 3 July, I contacted the
Whittier Police Department.  I witnessed multiple pedestrian and vehicle interactions
along Hightower Road as a result of Safeway's refrigerated truck. It is parked
perpendicular to Hightower and blocks the sideway and partway into Hightower Road.

On 3 July, Safeway staff sporadically unloaded items until 10 AM and then closed up the

truck; it remains.

Within the municipality, obstructing a collector road requires a permit. When prompted,
Safeway staff conveyed they had no permit because they would be actively unloading all
weekend.  I read up on municipal code, and that's not a true statement. There was no
traffic plan, no cones, no notification, nothing to abate the impact.

In addition to the safety hazard:
1. The truck's refrigeration unit is above the permitted decibels across from a residential
building.
2. The truck blocked multiple business' storefronts from potential foot traffic.

On 7 July, I followed up with Whittier Police. They conveyed that an Officer stopped by
and took the active loading comment at face value.  I am disappointed at the lack of
code awareness that gave the office standing to remove the hazard.

I recall Safeway's need to have a refrigerated truck last year due to the broken freezers;
that is not the impetus this year. Safeway has another loading dock capability over by its
trash cans and the vendor it permits to set up in their property.

Please let me know what I may do to ensure this does not occur again.

--


- Christina

Community Concerns for follow-up

DOT Items:
DOT Alyeska Highway Pedestrian Safety Corridor (Bike Path) concerns:
Refresh of painted stencils: GVSA manager has approval from DOT for approval for GVSA to re-paint
stencils. Bollards: GVSA will continue to use bollards seasonally to restrict vehicles from path. Bollards
are removed in winter to allow for snow clearing.

GVSA does not have authority or funding mechanism to work on DOT ROW without permission by
DOT. Directive to lower the speed limit to 40MPH zone and extend the 30MPH zone, pending
information on timeline and infrastructure countermeasures by DOT to support these changes.

Community interest in traffic calming in the 45MPH zone: request to lower speed limit to 30MPH and
to add flashing radar “You are Speeding” signage. GBOS resolution of Support was recommended by
PSAC in November 2024; resolution 2025-03 was signed and sent to SOA in Jan 2025.

Unrestricted access to airport property. Public should call police to report illegal activity. No
recreational access is permitted on airport land. Service Area stated that 2nd gate after the hangar
condo to be added to deter parties. DOT is examining this request. Local pilot says that DOT is
considering gate just after the last residence on Donner Rd, where airport property begins.

Enforcement Concerns:
Drug/Alcohol use in Girdwood Parks – Chief Achee will have patrol include walk-thru.
Alyeska Highway Speeding. Speed limit enforcement by Whittier Police requested for 45MPH zone.
Unsafe parking on roads - Call Whittier Police for parking enforcement if emergency vehicles are
unable to pass. WPD has equipment and authority to enforce municipal parking laws.

Homeless Camps:
Abatement of homeless camps completed spring 2024 and illegal parking has been enforced
successfully since then within the Service Area. Starting in 2026 surcharge assessed at dump funds
Healthy Spaces team, which respond to public land that needs to be cleaned up. Report Camp or
Trash Concern

              Special Activity Report - Fourth of July Weekend

                                   Reporting Period: July 3-5, 2026
Executive Summary
During the July 4th weekend reporting period, WPD documented 79 total calls for service from July 3 through July 5,
2026. Activity was concentrated in Girdwood with 59 calls (75%), followed by Whittier with 17 calls (22%) and Other
areas with 3 calls (4%). Security checks accounted for 29 calls and are included in the total call count; excluding
security checks, officers handled 50 operational calls.

Key Points
•   Total calls: 79 over the three-day holiday weekend.
•   Operational calls excluding security checks: 50.
•   Traffic-related activity was the largest operational category with 17 calls, including traffic stops, traffic
    enforcement, REDDI/reckless driving, traffic complaints, and traffic hazards.
•   Proactive activity remained high with 29 security checks and 5 foot patrols.
•   Notable calls included 2 hit-and-run reports, 3 medical calls, 1 fireworks complaint, 1 welfare check, 1
    trespassing call, 1 missing person call, and 1 physical fight.
•  No death-related call type was identified in the provided data.

Narrative Summary
The July 4th weekend produced a mix of holiday-related public safety activity, proactive patrols, traffic enforcement,
and routine calls for service. Girdwood accounted for the majority of documented activity, with a substantial number
of security checks, foot patrols, traffic calls, parking problems, noise complaints, and two hit-and-run related calls.
Whittier activity included public assists, medical calls, traffic enforcement, a fireworks complaint, a welfare check,
trespassing, a missing person call, and other service-related responses.

Traffic-related calls were the leading operational category. The dataset included traffic stops, traffic enforcement,
reckless driving complaints, a REDDI report, a traffic hazard, and a traffic complaint. This indicates a significant
enforcement and roadway-safety component during the holiday weekend.

Security checks were a major portion of the call volume and appear to reflect proactive area checks during the
holiday period. These checks were especially concentrated in Girdwood, including Alyeska, Arlberg, Hightower,
Mount Hood, Toadstool, Lindblad, Egloff, and Seward Highway-area locations. Whittier security check activity was
also documented.
